notes: Arms ran as host subagents (no cursor-agent CLI on this machine) inside throwaway fixture repos built by skills/ticket-workflow/evals/fixtures/setup-eval-*.sh; each arm got a fresh fixture instance under mktemp -d.
The with_skill arm received SKILL.md plus the eval's with_skill_references embedded inline; the without_skill arm received only the task. Neither arm saw the assertions.

Isolation caveat: both arms shared the host harness, so the workspace AGENTS.md and the skill's frontmatter description were visible in the subagents' system context despite prompt-level prohibitions on using them. Baseline outputs show no skill vocabulary (status open/todo, no Outcome blocks, no hex IDs, no worktrees), so no material leakage was observed.
Timing and token metrics were unavailable from subagent completion notifications; this benchmark compares output quality only.

Grading was performed by the orchestrating agent against the assertion list only, preferring file inspection, git history, and post-hoc command execution on the live fixtures; 2 of 32 assertions (both in eval 1) partially relied on run-report text and carry judge-bias caveats recorded in the grading.json files.
Run reports proved unreliable in 4 of 6 runs (claimed sections/fields/filenames diverging from committed artifacts); all grades were anchored to artifacts.

analyst_observations: The skill's value concentrates in convention-shaped behavior: lifecycle vocabulary, template sections, Outcome schema, commit discipline, and the entire epic scaffolding protocol (hex IDs, worktree+branch isolation, closure ticket, orchestration prompt). A strong baseline reproduces none of these unprompted.

The baseline is substantively competent: it honored explicit dependency metadata, scoped changes correctly, never swept decoy files, and in eval 2 produced excellent generic decomposition (binding interface contracts, wave scheduling). Convention conformance, not engineering judgment, is what the skill buys at frontier-model tier.

The dependency hard-stop did not discriminate because the fixture declared the dependency explicitly in frontmatter and in ticket constraints; a subtler design (bare cross-epic ID with a tempting global match, or an in-progress dependency) is needed to test the skill's resolution rules specifically.

The baseline durably marked the blocked ticket `status: blocked` with an in-ticket note, while the with_skill arm only reported the blocker in chat - SKILL.md says 'STOP and report' without specifying a durable location. Skill gap worth folding back.

Run-report narratives diverged from committed artifacts in 4 of 6 runs (phantom sections, phantom complexity value, wrong filenames). Artifact-based grading is mandatory; self-reports alone would have flipped at least one assertion in each arm.
